profile.reading:
Meta broke ground on 11 February 2026 on a data center campus in the LEAP Research and Innovation District in Lebanon, Boone County, Indiana, about 29 miles northwest of downtown Indianapolis. Meta says the site is designed for 1 GW of capacity and represents an investment of more than $10 billion. It is Meta's second Indiana site after Jeffersonville.

The approved plan has 13 buildings, ten of them data center buildings, totalling about 4 million square feet. The campus sits in the southern part of the district, west of Interstate 65 and crossed by State Road 32. Meta expects the first buildings online by the end of 2027, with about 300 operating jobs.

Meta says it will pay the full cost of its energy and use a closed-loop liquid cooling system. City documents called the project Project Domino. No street address has been published, so the facility is not yet mapped.

reading.body:
Meta's Lebanon, Indiana campus is a 1 GW, $10 billion, 4 million square foot bet that AI capacity is now planned in gigawatts and paid for up front. The announced design capacity is the number that matters, because it sets the power the site must secure before any of its ten data center buildings can run.

The physical scale is the constraint made visible. Thirteen buildings across roughly 4 million square feet, sited on State Road 32 west of Interstate 65 in Boone County, about 29 miles northwest of Indianapolis, with first buildings expected online by the end of 2027. Meta says it will pay the full cost of its energy and use closed-loop liquid cooling, which is a statement about both the power bill and the water and heat problem that dense AI racks create.

What the data does not cover is the part that decides whether the timeline holds. There is no published interconnection agreement, no generation source, no transmission upgrade, and no street address, so the facility is not mapped. The 1 GW figure is a design target, not a measured draw, and the record notes published IT capacity as missing. The 300 operating jobs are the only employment figure given, and they say nothing about construction labor or the surrounding grid.

Read against the rest of the sector, this is one more confirmation that the binding question for AI is not chip supply but whether a site can be wired to enough power by a stated date. Lebanon gives a date, an investment, and a capacity target. It does not yet give the supply behind them.
